title: Engineering
blurb: Forces, machines and the shapes that keep structures standing.

lessons.title: Forces, levers & gears
lessons.summary: Why a long spanner works, and how machines trade force for distance.

cards.title: Force, mass and weight
cards.text: A force makes a mass accelerate. Weight is just the force of gravity on a mass: W = m × g, with g ≈ 9.81 m/s² on Earth. Mass is measured in kg; force and weight in newtons (N).

cards.title: Levers multiply force
cards.text:
Turning effect, or torque, is force × distance from the pivot. A small force far from the pivot balances a large force close to it.

That's why a long spanner loosens a stuck bolt, and why door handles sit far from the hinges.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><rect class="s bgf" x="16" y="146" width="288" height="5" rx="2"/><path class="s bgf" d="M180 151 L165 175 H195 Z"/><rect class="s bgf" x="48" y="122" width="24" height="24" rx="3"/><rect class="s bgf" x="200" y="102" width="40" height="44" rx="3"/><path class="a" d="M60 162L166 162"/><path class="a" d="M194 162L220 162"/><path class="a" d="M60 157L60 167"/><path class="a" d="M220 157L220 167"/></g><text class="" x="60" y="116" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:17px">2 kg</text><text class="" x="220" y="96" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:17px">6 kg</text><text class="a" x="112" y="176" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">3 m</text><text class="a" x="207" y="176" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">1 m</text><text class="r" x="160" y="34" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:20px">2 × 3 = 6 × 1 → balanced</text></svg>

cards.title: Try it: balance the seesaw
cards.text: The right side holds 6 kg at 1 m from the pivot. Change the mass and distance on the left until the beam levels out.

cards.title: Pulleys trade distance for force
cards.text:
With a moving pulley, the load hangs from two strands of rope, so each strand carries half the weight. You pull with half the force, but you have to pull twice as much rope.

The work you do, force × distance, stays the same. Machines never give energy for free; they let you choose how to spend it.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><path class="s" d="M20 20L300 20"/><path class="s" d="M40 20L32 12"/><path class="s" d="M58 20L50 12"/><path class="s" d="M76 20L68 12"/><path class="s" d="M94 20L86 12"/><path class="s" d="M112 20L104 12"/><path class="s" d="M130 20L122 12"/><path class="s" d="M148 20L140 12"/><path class="s" d="M166 20L158 12"/><path class="s" d="M184 20L176 12"/><path class="s" d="M202 20L194 12"/><path class="s" d="M220 20L212 12"/><path class="s" d="M238 20L230 12"/><path class="s" d="M256 20L248 12"/><path class="s" d="M274 20L266 12"/><path class="s" d="M292 20L284 12"/><path class="s" d="M144 20L144 32"/><circle class="s" cx="144" cy="50" r="18"/><circle class="s" cx="180" cy="125" r="18"/><path class="a" d="M198 20 V125 A18 18 0 0 1 162 125 V50 A18 18 0 0 0 126 50 V150"/><path class="s" d="M180 143L180 150"/><rect class="s bgf" x="160" y="150" width="40" height="24" rx="3"/><path class="r" d="M110 120L110 162"/><path class="r" d="M106.5 154.8L110 162L113.5 154.8"/></g><text class="r" x="102" y="150" text-anchor="end" style="font-size:17px">pull 1 m</text><text class="" x="208" y="168" text-anchor="start" style="font-size:16px">load rises ½ m</text></svg>

cards.title: Gears: speed or torque
cards.text:
When a small gear drives a big one, the big gear turns slower but with more torque. The ratio is the number of teeth: 10 teeth driving 20 gives half the speed and twice the torque.

A bike's low gear, a drill's gearbox and a car's first gear all use this trade.

cards.title: Balanced and unbalanced forces
cards.text: When forces on an object balance, it stays still or keeps moving at a steady speed. When they don't, it accelerates in the direction of the net force.

cards.title: Inclined planes
example: Lift 100 kg 1 m using a 4 m ramp
cards.text: A ramp lets you raise a load with less force by pushing it over a longer distance. The force needed is roughly the weight times the height divided by the length.

cards.title: Screws and wedges
cards.text: A screw is a ramp wrapped around a cylinder: each turn moves it forward a little with great force. A wedge (an axe, a chisel) turns a push into a sideways splitting force.

cards.title: Mechanical advantage
cards.text: Mechanical advantage is output force divided by input force. A lever with MA = 5 lets you lift 5 times what you push, but you move 5 times farther.

cards.title: Torque in practice
cards.text: Bolts are tightened to a specified torque in newton-metres. A wheel nut on a car is often around 100–140 N·m: 400 N on a 30 cm wrench gives 120 N·m.

quiz.q: A 50 kg person stands on a scale. Their weight is about…
4 kg sits 1.5 m from the pivot. How far from the pivot must 2 kg sit to balance?
A 12-tooth gear drives a 36-tooth gear. The output turns…
quiz.explain: The ratio is 36 ÷ 12 = 3: one third of the speed, three times the torque.

quiz.q: To lift 200 kg by 1 m with a 5 m ramp (no friction) you need about…
A torque wrench set to 120 N·m with a 0.4 m handle needs a force of…

lessons.title: How structures stand up
lessons.summary: Tension, compression and the shapes engineers use to manage them.

cards.title: Tension and compression
cards.text:
Load a beam in the middle and it bends. The top gets squeezed (compression) and the bottom gets stretched (tension). Somewhere in between is a neutral line that feels neither.

Concrete is strong in compression but weak in tension, which is why beams have steel bars near the bottom.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><path class="s bgf" d="M30 95 Q160 125 290 95 L290 115 Q160 145 30 115 Z"/><path class="s" d="M40 112 L30 132 H50 Z"/><path class="s" d="M280 112 L270 132 H290 Z"/><path class="r" d="M160 40L160 100"/><path class="r" d="M156.5 92.8L160 100L163.5 92.8"/><path class="a" d="M70 82L118 92"/><path class="a" d="M111.2 93.7L118 92L112.5 87.7"/><path class="a" d="M250 82L202 92"/><path class="a" d="M207.5 87.7L202 92L208.8 93.7"/><path class="r" d="M130 156L84 144"/><path class="r" d="M90.9 142.6L84 144L89.3 148.5"/><path class="r" d="M190 156L236 144"/><path class="r" d="M230.7 148.5L236 144L229.1 142.6"/></g><text class="r" x="160" y="30" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:17px">load</text><text class="a" x="70" y="70" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">compression</text><text class="a" x="250" y="70" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">compression</text><text class="r" x="160" y="174" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:17px">tension</text></svg>

cards.title: Why engineers love triangles
cards.text:
Push the corner of a square frame and it folds into a parallelogram; the joints just rotate. A triangle can't change shape without changing the length of a side.

That's why cranes, roof trusses, pylons and bike frames are made of triangles.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><path class="dash" d="M50 50 H140 L120 140 H30 Z"/><rect class="s" x="30" y="50" width="90" height="90" rx="0"/><path class="r" d="M6 40L46 40"/><path class="r" d="M38.8 43.5L46 40L38.8 36.5"/><path class="s" d="M190 140 L250 50 L310 140 Z"/><path class="r" d="M205 40L245 40"/><path class="r" d="M237.8 43.5L245 40L237.8 36.5"/><circle class="fi" cx="30" cy="50" r="4"/><circle class="fi" cx="120" cy="50" r="4"/><circle class="fi" cx="120" cy="140" r="4"/><circle class="fi" cx="30" cy="140" r="4"/><circle class="fi" cx="190" cy="140" r="4"/><circle class="fi" cx="250" cy="50" r="4"/><circle class="fi" cx="310" cy="140" r="4"/></g><text class="" x="75" y="168" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:18px">square folds</text><text class="a" x="250" y="168" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:18px">triangle holds</text></svg>

cards.title: Arches push outward
cards.text:
An arch turns a downward load into compression that runs around its curve to the ground. Stone, which is strong in compression, is perfect for it.

The catch is that the feet push outward. Without solid abutments or a tie between the feet, the arch spreads and collapses.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><rect class="s bgf" x="20" y="130" width="50" height="40" rx="0"/><rect class="s bgf" x="250" y="130" width="50" height="40" rx="0"/><path class="s" d="M45 130 Q160 -10 275 130"/><path class="s" d="M70 130 Q160 30 250 130"/><path class="r" d="M160 12L160 54"/><path class="r" d="M156.5 46.8L160 54L163.5 46.8"/><path class="a" d="M62 124L26 146"/><path class="a" d="M30.3 139.3L26 146L34 145.2"/><path class="a" d="M258 124L294 146"/><path class="a" d="M286 145.2L294 146L289.7 139.3"/></g><text class="r" x="172" y="22" text-anchor="start" style="font-size:17px">load</text><text class="a" x="160" y="168" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:17px">feet push outward</text></svg>

cards.title: The I-beam
cards.text:
When a beam bends, the most stress is at the top and bottom faces and very little in the middle. An I-beam puts most of its steel in the top and bottom flanges and joins them with a thin web.

You get almost the stiffness of a solid block with a fraction of the weight.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><rect class="y" x="96" y="28" width="128" height="28" rx="4" transform="rotate(-1.2 96 28)"/><rect class="y" x="96" y="136" width="128" height="28" rx="4" transform="rotate(-1.2 96 136)"/><rect class="s bgf" x="100" y="30" width="120" height="22" rx="1"/><rect class="s bgf" x="150" y="52" width="20" height="86" rx="0"/><rect class="s bgf" x="100" y="138" width="120" height="22" rx="1"/></g><text class="r" x="50" y="46" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">high stress</text><text class="r" x="50" y="154" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">high stress</text><text class="" x="60" y="100" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">low stress</text><text class="a" x="232" y="46" text-anchor="start" style="font-size:17px">flange</text><text class="a" x="182" y="100" text-anchor="start" style="font-size:17px">web</text><text class="a" x="232" y="154" text-anchor="start" style="font-size:17px">flange</text></svg>

cards.title: Factor of safety
cards.text:
Engineers never design right up to the breaking point. Materials vary, loads get underestimated and things wear out. The factor of safety is how much stronger something is than it needs to be.

Lifting gear often uses 4 or 5; aircraft structures use about 1.5, because extra weight costs fuel and every part is tested closely.
example: Hook rated for 1 t, breaks at 4 t
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><rect class="fpen" x="30" y="56" width="70" height="26" rx="3"/><rect class="fred" x="30" y="104" width="280" height="26" rx="3"/></g><text class="a" x="110" y="75" text-anchor="start" style="font-size:17px">rated 1 t</text><text class="tp" x="40" y="123" text-anchor="start" style="font-size:17px">breaks at 4 t</text><text class="" x="160" y="165" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:18px">4 ÷ 1 = factor of safety 4</text></svg>

cards.title: Cantilevers
cards.text: A cantilever is supported at one end only: balconies, diving boards, shelf brackets. The top is in tension and the bottom in compression, the opposite of a simply supported beam.

cards.title: Columns and buckling
cards.text: A tall slender column doesn't crush; it buckles sideways first. Doubling its length can cut its buckling load to a quarter, which is why columns are braced.

cards.title: Shells and domes
cards.text: Curved shells spread loads through their surface, like an eggshell. Domes from the Pantheon in Rome to modern stadiums cover huge spaces with little material.

cards.title: Load paths
cards.text: Every load must travel down through the structure to the ground: floor to beams, beams to columns, columns to foundations. If any link is missing, something fails.

cards.title: Dead, live and environmental loads
cards.text: Engineers design for dead load (the structure's own weight), live load (people, furniture, snow), and environmental loads like wind and earthquakes, then add safety factors.

quiz.q: A simply supported beam carries a load in the middle. Where is it in tension?
quiz.explain: It sags, so the bottom stretches (tension) and the top squeezes (compression).

quiz.q: Why are trusses made of triangles?
options: They use less steel than squares
A triangle can't deform without a side changing length
quiz.explain: Fixed side lengths lock a triangle's angles, so pinned joints alone keep it rigid.

quiz.q: Rope with a breaking load of 600 kg, used with a factor of safety of 5. Max working load?
quiz.explain: Working load = failure load ÷ FoS = 600 ÷ 5 = 120 kg.

quiz.q: A balcony fixed only at the wall is a…
What usually makes a tall slender column fail?

lessons.title: Engineering materials
lessons.summary: Steel, concrete, wood, aluminium and plastics.

cards.title: Strength and stiffness are different

items: steel stiff, aluminium a third as stiff

cards.text: Strength is how much stress a material takes before it breaks or yields. Stiffness is how much it resists bending or stretching. Rubber is weak and flexible; glass is stiff but brittle.

cards.title: Steel
cards.text: Steel is iron with a little carbon. It's strong in both tension and compression, ductile (bends before breaking) and recyclable, but heavy and rusts without protection.

cards.title: Concrete
cards.text: Concrete is cement, water, sand and gravel. It's cheap and very strong in compression but weak in tension, so steel bars (rebar) are added where tension occurs.

cards.title: Wood
cards.text: Wood is strong along the grain and weak across it. For its weight it's remarkably strong, it stores carbon and is easy to work, but moisture, fire and insects must be managed.

cards.title: Aluminium
cards.text: Aluminium is about a third the weight of steel and doesn't rust (a thin oxide layer protects it). It's less stiff, so parts are made thicker or shaped cleverly. Used in aircraft, window frames, cars.

cards.title: Plastics and composites
cards.text: Plastics are light, cheap and mouldable. Composites like carbon fibre embed strong fibres in resin, giving very high strength and stiffness for their weight: bikes, aircraft, racing cars.

cards.title: Choosing a material
cards.text: Engineers weigh strength, stiffness, weight, cost, durability, ease of manufacture and environmental impact. There's never a perfect material, only the best compromise.

cards.title: Embodied carbon
cards.text: Making cement releases a lot of CO₂, about 8% of global emissions according to many estimates. Steel production is also carbon-heavy. That's driving interest in timber buildings and low-carbon cements.

cards.title: Corrosion
cards.text: Steel rusts when exposed to oxygen and water, especially with salt. Protection includes paint, galvanising (zinc coating), stainless alloys and keeping concrete cover over rebar.

cards.title: Glass
cards.text: Glass is very strong in compression but brittle: a tiny scratch can start a crack. Tempered glass is heat-treated to be much stronger and shatters into small blunt pieces; laminated glass holds together.

quiz.q: Why does reinforced concrete contain steel bars?
options: Concrete is weak in tension, so steel carries the tensile forces

quiz.q: Wood is strongest…
Which is the lightest per volume?
quiz.explain: Aluminium is about a third of steel's density.

lessons.title: Stress and strain
lessons.summary: How materials stretch, bend and break.

cards.title: Stress
example: 10 kN on a 100 mm² steel bar
cards.text: Stress is force divided by the area carrying it. The same force on a thinner bar creates more stress. Units: pascals (N/m²), usually megapascals (MPa).

cards.title: Strain
cards.text: Strain is how much a material stretches compared with its original length. It has no units and is usually tiny.

cards.title: Young's modulus
cards.text: Stiffness is measured by Young's modulus: stress divided by strain. Steel is about 200 GPa, aluminium about 70, wood about 10 along the grain.

cards.title: Elastic and plastic
cards.text: In the elastic range, a material springs back when unloaded. Past the yield point it deforms permanently (plastic). Engineers design structures to stay elastic in normal use.

cards.title: The stress–strain curve
cards.text: Testing a steel bar in a machine draws a curve: a straight elastic line, a yield point, then plastic stretching up to the ultimate strength, and finally fracture.

cards.title: Ductile vs brittle
cards.text: Ductile materials (steel, copper) stretch a lot before breaking, giving warning. Brittle ones (glass, cast iron, concrete) snap suddenly. Ductility makes structures safer.

cards.title: Bending stress
cards.text: When a beam bends, stress is zero at the middle (neutral axis) and greatest at the top and bottom surfaces. That's why I-beams put material far from the middle.

cards.title: Second moment of area
cards.text: A beam's resistance to bending depends hugely on its depth. For a rectangle, doubling the depth makes it eight times stiffer. That's why joists are placed on edge.

cards.title: Thermal expansion
cards.text: Materials grow when heated. A 100 m steel bridge can lengthen about 4 cm between winter and summer, so it has expansion joints. Rails, pipes and concrete slabs need room to move too.

cards.title: Stress concentrations

items.w: square window in a pressurised cabin

cards.text: Sharp corners, holes and notches concentrate stress, sometimes to three times the average. Rounded corners (fillets) spread it out. Aircraft windows are rounded for this reason.

quiz.q: 20 kN on a 400 mm² bar gives a stress of…
Turning a plank on edge makes it much stiffer because…
options: Bending stiffness grows with depth cubed

quiz.q: Which material gives warning before breaking?

lessons.title: Friction
lessons.summary: The force that grips, slows and wears things down.

cards.title: What friction is
cards.text: Friction resists sliding between surfaces. At a microscopic level, even smooth surfaces are rough, and bumps catch and briefly bond.

cards.title: Coefficient of friction
cards.text: Friction force is roughly the normal force (how hard surfaces press together) times a coefficient μ that depends on the materials.

cards.title: Static vs kinetic
cards.text: It takes more force to start something sliding than to keep it going. Static friction is higher than kinetic (sliding) friction. That's why ABS keeps wheels from locking.

cards.title: Brakes
cards.text: Brakes turn motion into heat through friction between pads and discs. On a long descent, brakes can overheat and fade; using engine braking or EV regeneration helps.

cards.title: Tyres and grip
cards.text: Tyres grip through friction and slight deformation of the rubber. On wet roads, tread grooves channel water away; without them, the tyre can aquaplane on a water film.

cards.title: Lubrication
cards.text: Oil and grease separate surfaces with a thin film, cutting friction and wear dramatically. Engines, bearings and gearboxes depend on it.

cards.title: Bearings
cards.text: Ball and roller bearings replace sliding with rolling, which has far lower friction. They're in wheels, motors, fans and hard drives.

cards.title: Useful friction
cards.text: Without friction you couldn't walk, drive, hold a pen or keep a nut on a bolt. Engineers often add friction on purpose: clutch plates, belt drives, non-slip floors.

cards.title: Rolling resistance
cards.text: Even rolling tyres lose energy as the rubber flexes. Low-rolling-resistance tyres and correct pressure save fuel or EV range.

cards.title: Wear costs

items.l: of world energy used to overcome friction (estimate)

cards.text: Friction and wear are estimated to consume around a fifth of the world's energy and cause large losses through worn parts, according to tribology studies. Better lubricants and materials save a lot.

quiz.q: A 50 kg box (≈490 N) on a floor with μ = 0.4 needs about how much force to slide?
Why is it harder to start pushing a box than to keep it moving?
options: Static friction is higher than kinetic friction
quiz.explain: Starting needs to overcome static friction.

quiz.q: What do ball bearings do?
quiz.explain: Rolling resists far less than sliding.

lessons.title: Work, energy and power
lessons.summary: Lifting, moving and how fast it happens.

cards.title: Work
cards.text: Work is done when a force moves something: force times distance. Lift a 10 kg bag 1 m and you do about 98 J of work.

cards.title: Potential energy
cards.text: Raising something stores energy that can be released when it falls. Hydroelectric dams use this with millions of tonnes of water.

cards.title: Kinetic energy
example: 1,500 kg car at 50 km/h vs 100 km/h
cards.text: Moving objects carry energy that grows with the square of speed. Double the speed and the energy quadruples, which is why speed matters so much in crashes.

cards.title: Power
cards.text: Power is how fast work is done: joules per second, or watts. A strong cyclist sustains about 200–300 W; a car engine delivers tens to hundreds of kW.

cards.title: Horsepower
cards.text: James Watt defined horsepower to sell steam engines: about 746 W in the imperial version. The metric horsepower (cv in Portugal) is about 735 W.

cards.title: Efficiency
cards.text: No machine converts all input energy into useful output; some becomes heat or noise. Efficiency is useful output divided by input.

cards.title: Energy is conserved

steps: Top of the hill: potential energy

cards.text: Energy changes form but the total stays the same. A falling roller coaster turns potential energy into kinetic energy, then back again, minus friction losses.

cards.title: Joules and kWh
cards.text: Engineers use joules; electricity bills use kWh. One kWh is 3.6 million joules, the energy of a 1 kW heater running for an hour.

cards.title: Energy in fuels
cards.text: A litre of petrol holds about 9 kWh of chemical energy, which is why liquid fuels were so hard to beat. Lithium batteries hold far less per kilo, but electric drivetrains use energy much more efficiently.

cards.title: Springs
cards.text: A spring stores energy when stretched or compressed. Its force is proportional to how far it moves (Hooke's law), used in suspensions, scales and clocks.

quiz.q: Kinetic energy at 100 km/h compared with 50 km/h is…
Lifting 20 kg by 2 m does about how much work?
1 kWh equals…

lessons.title: Fluids and hydraulics
lessons.summary: Pressure, buoyancy and the power of liquids.

cards.title: Pressure
cards.text: Pressure is force spread over an area. A stiletto heel presses far harder on the floor than an elephant's foot, because the area is tiny.

cards.title: Pressure in water
cards.text: Water pressure increases with depth, about 1 bar every 10 metres. Divers feel it in their ears; dams are thicker at the bottom for the same reason.

cards.title: Atmospheric pressure
cards.text: Air above us presses down with about 1 bar (101 kPa) at sea level, roughly 10 tonnes on every square metre. We don't notice because it pushes equally from all sides.

cards.title: Pascal's principle
cards.text: Pressure in a closed liquid spreads equally in all directions. Push a small piston and a big piston feels the same pressure over a larger area, giving a bigger force.

cards.title: Hydraulics everywhere
cards.text: Car brakes, excavators, lifts and presses use hydraulic fluid to multiply force and transmit it through flexible hoses.

cards.title: Buoyancy
cards.text: An object in a fluid is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of fluid it displaces (Archimedes). If that's more than its own weight, it floats. Steel ships float because their shape displaces a lot of water.

cards.title: Flow in pipes
cards.text: Flow rate equals speed times pipe area. Squeeze a hose and the water speeds up. Narrow pipes need more pressure to push the same flow because of friction.

cards.title: Bernoulli
cards.text: Where a fluid moves faster, its pressure drops. This helps explain carburettors, atomisers and part of how wings and sails create lift.

cards.title: Siphons
cards.text: A siphon moves liquid up over a barrier and down to a lower point without a pump, as long as the outlet is below the source and the tube starts full.

cards.title: Viscosity
cards.text: Viscosity is a fluid's thickness: honey is viscous, water isn't. Oil grades like 5W-30 describe how viscosity behaves when cold (5W) and hot (30).

quiz.q: Roughly how much does pressure increase per 10 m of water depth?
A hydraulic jack with an area ratio of 20 turns 50 N into…
Why does a steel ship float?
options: Its shape displaces a weight of water greater than its own

lessons.title: How planes fly
lessons.summary: Lift, drag, thrust and weight.

cards.title: Four forces
cards.text: In steady flight, lift balances weight and thrust balances drag. To climb, lift exceeds weight; to speed up, thrust exceeds drag.

cards.title: How wings make lift
cards.text: A wing is shaped and tilted (angle of attack) to deflect air downwards. Pushing air down pushes the wing up (Newton's third law), with lower pressure above the wing and higher below.

cards.title: The lift equation

viz.f: L = ½ × ρ × v² × S × CL

cards.text: Lift grows with air density, wing area and the square of speed. That's why planes need long runways at hot, high airports where air is thin.

cards.title: Stall
cards.text: Increase the angle of attack too much and the airflow separates from the upper surface. Lift collapses suddenly: a stall. Pilots train to recognise and recover from it.

cards.title: Flaps and slats
cards.text: For take-off and landing, flaps and slats extend from the wing to increase its area and curvature, giving more lift at low speed.

cards.title: Drag
cards.text: Drag comes from friction with the air and from the pressure difference behind the object. It grows with the square of speed, so going faster costs a lot more fuel.

cards.title: Jet engines

steps: Turbine and exhaust push the plane

cards.text: A turbofan sucks in air, compresses it, burns fuel in it and blasts the hot gas out the back. Most thrust in airliners comes from the big fan pushing air around the core.

cards.title: Why airliners cruise high
cards.text: At about 10–12 km altitude, the air is thin, so drag is much lower and jet engines are more efficient. Cabins are pressurised to the equivalent of about 2,000 m.

cards.title: Control surfaces
cards.text: Ailerons on the wings roll the plane, the elevator on the tail pitches it up and down, and the rudder yaws it left and right.

cards.title: Drones
cards.text: Multirotor drones have no wings; they create lift by spinning propellers. They steer by speeding up some motors and slowing others, with a flight controller adjusting hundreds of times a second.

quiz.q: What happens in a stall?
options: The wing's airflow separates and lift drops sharply
quiz.explain: Too high an angle of attack.

quiz.q: Doubling speed changes drag by a factor of about…
Which control surface rolls the plane?
quiz.explain: Ailerons move in opposite directions on each wing.

lessons.title: Bridges
lessons.summary: Beam, arch, suspension and cable-stayed.

cards.title: The main bridge types
cards.text: Bridges handle loads differently: beams bend, arches compress, suspension cables pull, and cable-stayed towers hold the deck with straight cables.

cards.title: Beam bridges
cards.text: The simplest bridge: a beam on supports. Cheap and quick for short spans, but deep beams are needed as the span grows, so they're often continuous over many piers.

cards.title: Arch bridges
cards.text: Arches carry loads in compression to strong abutments. Stone arches have lasted for 2,000 years. Porto's Dom Luís I bridge (1886) is a double-deck iron arch over the Douro.

cards.title: Suspension bridges
cards.text: Main cables hang from tall towers and are anchored at each end; vertical hangers hold the deck. They achieve the longest spans. Lisbon's 25 de Abril bridge (1966) is one.

cards.title: Cable-stayed bridges
cards.text: Straight cables run directly from towers to the deck in a fan or harp pattern. Efficient for medium-long spans and quick to build. Lisbon's Vasco da Gama bridge has a cable-stayed main span.

cards.title: Portuguese bridges
cards.text: Portugal has some remarkable bridges, including several by Gustave Eiffel's company and Edgar Cardoso.

cards.title: Wind and Tacoma Narrows
cards.text: In 1940 the Tacoma Narrows suspension bridge in the US twisted itself apart in a moderate wind, due to aerodynamic instability. Since then, decks are wind-tunnel tested and shaped to avoid it.

cards.title: Expansion joints
cards.text: Bridges grow and shrink with temperature. Expansion joints (the metal teeth you drive over) and sliding bearings let them move without cracking.

cards.title: Foundations in rivers

steps: Flood water speeds up around pier

cards.text: Piers in rivers must resist scour: fast water digging away the riverbed around them. Many bridge failures come from scour during floods, not from the structure itself.

cards.title: Inspection and maintenance
cards.text: Bridges are inspected regularly for cracks, corrosion, bearing wear and scour. Sensors increasingly monitor strain, vibration and movement in real time.

quiz.q: Which bridge type carries loads mainly in compression?
Lisbon's 25 de Abril bridge is a…
What destroyed the Tacoma Narrows bridge in 1940?

lessons.title: Buildings and foundations
lessons.summary: From the ground up.

cards.title: Why foundations?
cards.text: Foundations spread a building's weight onto soil that can carry it without sinking unevenly. The weaker the soil, the bigger or deeper the foundations.

cards.title: Shallow foundations
cards.text: Strip and pad footings, or a raft slab, work where firm soil or rock is near the surface. They're common for houses.

cards.title: Deep foundations
cards.text: On soft ground, piles are driven or drilled down to firmer layers, carrying loads by end bearing and friction along their sides. Lisbon's Baixa was rebuilt after 1755 on wooden piles.

cards.title: Settlement
cards.text: All buildings settle a little. Problems come from differential settlement, when one part sinks more than another, cracking walls and jamming doors.

cards.title: Walls and frames
cards.text: Traditional buildings have load-bearing walls of stone or brick. Modern ones use frames of concrete or steel columns and beams, with walls just filling the gaps.

cards.title: The Pombaline cage
cards.text: After the 1755 earthquake, Lisbon was rebuilt with the "gaiola pombalina": a timber lattice of diagonal braces inside masonry walls, one of the first earthquake-resistant building systems in Europe.

cards.title: Earthquake design
cards.text: Seismic codes require buildings to sway without collapsing: ductile connections, bracing, shear walls, regular shapes. Some use base isolators that let the ground move beneath them.

cards.title: Wind on tall buildings
cards.text: Wind pushes on tall buildings and makes them sway. Engineers stiffen them with cores and outriggers, and some skyscrapers use giant tuned mass dampers to cancel motion.

cards.title: Moisture and damp
cards.text: Water is the enemy of buildings: rising damp, leaks and condensation cause rot, mould and corrosion. Damp-proof courses, good roofs, gutters and ventilation keep it out.

cards.title: Burj Khalifa
cards.text: The world's tallest building, in Dubai, is 828 m high. Its Y-shaped plan and setbacks confuse the wind, and its foundations include 192 piles about 50 m long.

quiz.q: What is differential settlement?
options: One part of a building sinking more than another

quiz.q: What was the gaiola pombalina?
options: A timber lattice inside walls for earthquake resistance

quiz.q: When are piles used?
options: On solid rock near the surface
On soft ground, to reach firmer layers
quiz.explain: They transfer loads to deeper strata.

lessons.title: Engines
lessons.summary: How petrol and diesel engines turn fuel into motion.

cards.title: The four-stroke cycle
cards.text: Most car engines repeat four strokes: suck in air and fuel, squeeze it, ignite it so it pushes the piston, and push out the exhaust. "Suck, squeeze, bang, blow."

cards.title: Crankshaft
cards.text: Pistons move up and down; the crankshaft turns that into rotation, like legs pushing bicycle pedals. A flywheel smooths out the pulses.

cards.title: Petrol vs diesel
cards.text: Petrol engines use a spark to ignite the mixture. Diesels compress air so much that it gets hot enough to ignite fuel injected into it. Diesels are more efficient but heavier and produce more NOx and particles.

cards.title: Compression ratio
cards.text: Higher compression extracts more energy from the fuel. Petrol engines run about 10:1, diesels about 15–20:1. Too high in a petrol engine causes knocking.

cards.title: Turbochargers
cards.text: A turbo uses exhaust gas to spin a turbine that compresses intake air, forcing more air and fuel into the cylinders. Small engines can produce big power.

cards.title: Torque and power
cards.text: Torque is the twisting force; power is torque times rotational speed. Diesels deliver strong torque at low rpm; petrol engines often make peak power at high rpm.

cards.title: Gearboxes

items: keeps engine in its sweet spot

cards.text: Engines work best in a narrow speed range. Gears let the engine stay in that range whether the car is crawling or cruising. EV motors spin so widely they usually need just one gear.

cards.title: Cooling
cards.text: About a third of a fuel's energy leaves as heat through the cooling system, and another third through the exhaust. The radiator, coolant and thermostat keep the engine at its ideal temperature.

cards.title: Emissions control
cards.text: Catalytic converters turn carbon monoxide, unburnt fuel and NOx into less harmful gases. Diesel particulate filters trap soot; AdBlue reduces NOx in diesels.

cards.title: Hybrids
cards.text: Hybrids pair a combustion engine with an electric motor and battery, recovering braking energy and helping the engine work efficiently. Plug-in hybrids can drive tens of kilometres on electricity alone.

quiz.q: What ignites the fuel in a diesel engine?
What does a turbocharger use to compress intake air?
Roughly what share of fuel energy becomes useful work in a petrol car engine?
quiz.explain: The rest is lost as heat.

lessons.title: Engineering an electric car
lessons.summary: Battery, motor, inverter and thermal management.

cards.title: The drivetrain
cards.text: An EV has far fewer moving parts than a combustion car: a battery pack, an inverter that turns DC into three-phase AC, an electric motor and a single-speed reduction gear.

cards.title: The skateboard platform
cards.text: Most EVs mount the battery flat under the floor between the axles. That lowers the centre of gravity, frees cabin space and stiffens the body.

cards.title: Inverters
cards.text: The inverter switches the battery's DC on and off thousands of times a second with silicon or silicon-carbide transistors to create AC at whatever frequency the motor needs. Silicon carbide cuts losses, especially in 800 V cars.

cards.title: Thermal management
cards.text: Batteries like about 20–40 °C. Liquid cooling plates, heat pumps and pre-conditioning keep them there for fast charging and long life, and reuse waste heat to warm the cabin.

cards.title: Efficiency in kWh/100 km
cards.text: EV consumption is measured in kWh per 100 km. A compact car may use 14–16; a large SUV 20–24. Speed, cold and wind raise it a lot.

cards.title: Why range drops in winter

items: Battery chemistry slows in the cold

cards.text: Cold batteries have higher internal resistance, and heating the cabin takes energy. Range can fall by 20–30% in freezing weather; heat pumps reduce the loss.

cards.title: Aerodynamics
cards.text: At motorway speeds, most energy goes into pushing air. EVs have smooth underbodies, flush handles and low drag coefficients (Cd around 0.2–0.3).

cards.title: Regenerative braking
cards.text: The motor acts as a generator when slowing down, recovering part of the energy. Friction brakes are still there for hard stops and are used less, so they last much longer.

cards.title: Fewer parts, less maintenance

items: tyres, brake fluid, cabin filter, coolant

cards.text: No oil changes, spark plugs, clutch, exhaust or timing belt. Maintenance mostly involves tyres, brakes fluid, cabin filters and coolant.

cards.title: Battery warranties
cards.text: Most manufacturers guarantee batteries for about 8 years or 160,000 km, typically to at least 70% capacity. Real-world data shows most packs degrade slowly.

quiz.q: Which part converts the battery's DC into AC for the motor?
Why do EVs lose range in winter?
options: Cold batteries are less efficient and heating uses energy
quiz.explain: Both chemistry and cabin heating matter.

quiz.q: What's a typical drag coefficient for an efficient EV?

lessons.title: Thermodynamics
lessons.summary: Heat, engines and why nothing is 100% efficient.

cards.title: Temperature and heat
cards.text: Temperature measures how fast molecules jiggle. Heat is energy flowing from hotter to colder because of a temperature difference.

cards.title: Absolute zero
cards.text: Nothing can be colder than −273.15 °C, absolute zero, where molecular motion is at a minimum. The kelvin scale starts there: 0 K.

cards.title: First law
cards.text: Energy can't be created or destroyed. Heat added to a system goes into raising its internal energy or doing work.

cards.title: Second law
cards.text: Heat flows naturally from hot to cold, never the reverse on its own. Every real process creates some disorder (entropy), which is why no engine can turn all heat into work.

cards.title: Carnot efficiency

viz.f: η max = 1 − T cold ÷ T hot

example: Steam at 550 °C (823 K), river at 20 °C (293 K)
cards.text: The maximum possible efficiency of a heat engine depends only on its hot and cold temperatures, in kelvin.

cards.title: Heat engines and heat pumps
cards.text: A heat engine uses heat flow to make work. A heat pump does the reverse: uses work to move heat from cold to hot. Same physics, opposite direction.

cards.title: The refrigeration cycle
cards.text: A refrigerant evaporates in the cold side (absorbing heat), is compressed (getting hot), condenses in the hot side (releasing heat) and expands back. Fridges and heat pumps use this loop.

cards.title: Specific heat and storage
cards.text: Water stores a lot of heat per kilo, which makes it ideal for heating systems and thermal storage tanks. Stone and concrete store heat too: thermal mass keeps old houses cool in summer.

cards.title: Insulation and U-values
cards.text: Heat loss through walls is measured with U-values: watts lost per m² per degree of difference. Lower is better. A well-insulated modern wall may be below 0.3; an old solid wall can exceed 1.5.

cards.title: Phase changes
cards.text: Melting ice and boiling water absorb large amounts of energy without changing temperature. Turning 1 kg of water at 100 °C into steam takes about 2.26 MJ, over five times the energy to heat it from 0 to 100 °C.

quiz.q: What's the lowest possible temperature?
A heat pump uses work to…
options: Move heat from a colder place to a warmer one

quiz.q: A wall with a lower U-value…

lessons.title: Wood and carpentry
lessons.summary: Grain, moisture, joints and timber in construction.

cards.title: Hardwood and softwood
cards.text: Softwoods come from conifers (pine, spruce): fast-growing, light, used for structure. Hardwoods come from broadleaf trees (oak, chestnut, eucalyptus): usually denser and more durable.

cards.title: Moisture content
cards.text: Fresh-cut wood can be over 50% water by weight. It shrinks as it dries until it matches the air's humidity. Indoor timber should be dried to about 8–12% before use.

cards.title: Wood moves
cards.text: Wood shrinks and swells far more across the grain than along it. Doors stick in winter damp, floors gap in dry summers. Good carpentry leaves room for movement.

cards.title: Joints
cards.text: Traditional joints interlock pieces so the wood carries the load: mortise and tenon, dovetail, half-lap. Modern work also uses screws, dowels, biscuits and metal connectors.

cards.title: Reading the grain
cards.text: Plane and chisel with the grain, like stroking a cat, to avoid tear-out. Knots are weak points and can fall out of thin boards.

cards.title: Glulam and CLT
cards.text: Engineered timber glues layers together. Glulam makes long, strong beams; cross-laminated timber (CLT) panels have layers at right angles and can form walls and floors of multi-storey buildings.

cards.title: Protecting timber
cards.text: Rot needs moisture. Keep timber dry, ventilated and off the ground; use naturally durable species or treated wood outdoors. Woodworm and termites are managed with treatment and inspection.

cards.title: Timber in fire
cards.text: Thick timber chars on the outside, and the char layer insulates the core, so big beams keep their strength surprisingly long in a fire. Engineers design a char allowance into the sections.

cards.title: Roof structures
cards.text: Traditional Portuguese roofs use timber rafters and battens under ceramic tiles. Trusses spread the roof load to the walls; good ventilation stops condensation rot.

cards.title: Portugal's forests
cards.text: Eucalyptus, maritime pine and cork oak are Portugal's most common forest trees. Portugal is the world's largest cork producer, supplying roughly half the world's cork.

quiz.q: Why leave room for wood to move in a floor?
options: Wood shrinks and swells with humidity

quiz.q: Indoor timber should be dried to about…
Which country is the world's largest cork producer?
quiz.explain: Portugal supplies about half the world's cork.

lessons.title: Building a comfortable home
lessons.summary: Insulation, windows, thermal bridges and ventilation.

cards.title: The building envelope
cards.text: Walls, roof, floor and windows form the envelope that separates inside from outside. Its insulation, airtightness and shading decide how much energy the home needs.

cards.title: Where heat escapes
cards.text: In an uninsulated house, the roof often loses the most heat, followed by walls, windows and draughts. Insulating the roof first is usually the best value.

cards.title: External insulation (ETICS)
cards.text: Insulation boards fixed outside the walls and rendered over (the "capoto" system in Portugal) wrap the house in a continuous layer and keep the masonry warm, reducing thermal bridges.

cards.title: Thermal bridges
cards.text: A thermal bridge is a weak spot where heat bypasses the insulation: concrete beams, balcony slabs, window reveals. They cause cold spots, condensation and mould.

cards.title: Windows
cards.text: Double glazing with low-emissivity coating and a thermally broken frame loses far less heat than single glazing. External shading keeps summer sun out before it heats the room.

cards.title: Airtightness
cards.text: Uncontrolled draughts waste heat and carry moisture into walls. Sealing gaps around windows, pipes and roof junctions is cheap and effective.

cards.title: Ventilation
cards.text: A tight house needs controlled ventilation to remove moisture and stale air. Mechanical ventilation with heat recovery (MVHR) recovers most of the heat from the outgoing air.

cards.title: Condensation and mould
cards.text: Warm indoor air carries moisture; when it meets a cold surface, it condenses. Ventilation, insulation and avoiding cold spots prevent mould.

cards.title: Summer comfort
cards.text: In Portugal, keeping cool matters too: external blinds, shading, thermal mass, light colours and night ventilation often beat air conditioning.

cards.title: Energy certificates
cards.text: In Portugal, homes for sale or rent need an energy certificate (from A+ to F), issued through ADENE. It also recommends improvements.

quiz.q: Where does an uninsulated house often lose a large share of its heat, and is cheap to fix first?
quiz.explain: Roof insulation is usually the best first step.

quiz.q: What is a thermal bridge?
options: A weak spot where heat bypasses the insulation
quiz.explain: They cause cold spots and mould.

quiz.q: What does MVHR do?
options: Ventilates while recovering heat from outgoing air

lessons.title: Water in buildings
lessons.summary: Pressure, pumps, pipes and drainage.

cards.title: Water pressure at home
cards.text: Mains water usually arrives at about 2–5 bar. Too low and showers trickle; too high and taps hammer and appliances wear. A pressure-reducing valve fixes high pressure.

cards.title: Pipe sizing

viz.unit: flow at the same pressure loss (relative)

cards.text: Larger pipes carry more flow with less pressure loss. Long runs to an upstairs shower need bigger diameters than a short run to a basin.

cards.title: Pumps
cards.text: Centrifugal pumps spin an impeller to push water. Each has a curve: more flow means less pressure (head). Choose the pump where its curve meets your system's needs.

cards.title: Head and pressure

items.s: lift to a tank 20 m up

cards.text: Pump "head" is the height it can lift water. 10 m of head equals about 1 bar.

cards.title: Water hammer
cards.text: Closing a valve suddenly stops the flow, and the moving water's momentum creates a pressure spike that bangs pipes. Arrestors and slower-closing valves cure it.

cards.title: Hot water systems
cards.text: Water heaters store hot water in a tank (termoacumulador), or heat it instantly (gas or electric instantaneous). Solar thermal panels and heat pumps can supply most hot water in Portugal.

cards.title: Legionella
cards.text: Bacteria can grow in stored water between 25 and 45 °C. Storage tanks should reach about 60 °C periodically, and taps should deliver below scalding temperature with mixing valves.

cards.title: Drainage
cards.text: Drains work by gravity, so pipes need a fall (slope) of about 1–2%. Traps (U-bends) hold water to block sewer smells, and vents stop them from being sucked dry.

cards.title: Rainwater harvesting
cards.text: Collecting roof rainwater for toilets, gardens and washing machines saves mains water. A filter, a tank and a small pump are the main parts.

cards.title: Measuring water levels

steps: Ultrasonic sensor on the tank lid

cards.text: Tanks and wells are monitored with float switches, pressure sensors or ultrasonic sensors such as the JSN-SR04T, which send levels to a dashboard, even over LoRa from remote sites.

quiz.q: About how much pressure is 10 m of water head?
What causes water hammer?
options: Sudden valve closure stopping moving water

quiz.q: Why should hot water tanks reach about 60 °C periodically?

lessons.title: How things are made
lessons.summary: Casting, machining, forming, welding and 3D printing.

cards.title: Four families of processes
cards.text: Most manufacturing either removes material (machining), shapes it (forging, bending, casting), joins it (welding, bolting) or adds it layer by layer (3D printing).

cards.title: Casting
cards.text: Molten metal is poured into a mould and solidifies in its shape. Engine blocks, pump housings and art bronzes are cast. Die casting forces metal into steel moulds for mass production.

cards.title: Machining
cards.text: Lathes, mills and drills cut material away to precise shapes. CNC machines follow programmed paths and can hold tolerances of a few hundredths of a millimetre.

cards.title: Forming
cards.text: Sheet metal is bent, stamped and pressed into shape: car bodies, cans, enclosures. Forging hammers hot metal into shape, giving very strong parts like crankshafts.

cards.title: Injection moulding
cards.text: Melted plastic is injected into a steel mould and cools in seconds. Moulds are expensive, but each part then costs cents. Most plastic objects around you were made this way.

cards.title: Welding
cards.text: Welding melts the edges of two metal parts so they fuse. MIG is fast and easy; TIG is precise and clean; stick welding works outdoors. Good welds need clean metal and the right heat.

cards.title: 3D printing
cards.text: Additive manufacturing builds parts layer by layer. FDM printers melt plastic filament; resin printers cure liquid with light; metal printers fuse powder with lasers.

cards.title: Design for manufacture
cards.text: A part that's easy to design can be hard to make. Engineers adapt designs to the process: draft angles for moulding, standard drill sizes, minimum bend radii for sheet metal.

cards.title: Mass production
cards.text: Henry Ford's moving assembly line (1913) cut the time to build a Model T chassis from about 12 hours to about 1.5. Today's factories add robots, sensors and software.

cards.title: Quality control
cards.text: Factories measure parts with gauges, coordinate measuring machines and cameras. Statistical process control spots drift before parts go out of tolerance.

quiz.q: Which process is cheapest per part for very large volumes of plastic parts?
quiz.explain: Moulds are costly but each part is cheap.

quiz.q: What does a lathe make?
options: Round parts, by spinning the workpiece
quiz.explain: The workpiece rotates against the tool.

quiz.q: Forging makes parts that are…

lessons.title: Measurement and tolerances
lessons.summary: Units, precision and making parts fit.

cards.title: The SI system
cards.text: Engineering uses SI units: metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin. Derived units build on them: newton, pascal, joule, watt. Mixing units causes expensive mistakes.

cards.title: The Mars Climate Orbiter

items.w: one team in imperial, one in metric

cards.text: In 1999 NASA lost a €100-million-plus probe because one team used pound-force seconds and another expected newton-seconds. The spacecraft flew too low into Mars' atmosphere.

cards.title: Accuracy vs precision
cards.text: Accuracy is how close you are to the true value; precision is how consistent repeated measurements are. A tool can be precise but wrong if it's not calibrated.

cards.title: Tolerances
cards.text: No part is made exactly to size. A tolerance states the acceptable range, such as 20.00 ± 0.05 mm. Tighter tolerances cost more, so use them only where needed.

cards.title: Fits
cards.text: Shafts and holes are matched by fit: clearance (slides freely), transition (snug), or interference (pressed in). Standard fit systems like ISO 286 define them, such as H7/g6.

cards.title: Measuring tools
cards.text: A tape measures to about a millimetre; calipers to 0.02 mm; micrometers to 0.001 mm. Choose a tool at least ten times finer than the tolerance you're checking.

cards.title: Significant figures
cards.text: "2 m" and "2.000 m" mean different precision. Don't report more digits than your measurement supports; a calculator showing 3.14159 doesn't make a rough measurement precise.

cards.title: Calibration
cards.text: Instruments drift. Calibration compares them against a reference standard and corrects them. Torque wrenches, scales and pressure gauges in industry are calibrated on a schedule.

cards.title: Errors add up
cards.text: When parts stack together, their tolerances add. Ten parts each ±0.1 mm could, in the worst case, be off by ±1 mm together. Statistical tolerancing estimates the realistic spread.

cards.title: Imperial units still around
cards.text: Pipes, tyres, screens and some bolts still use inches; aviation uses feet and knots. One inch is exactly 25.4 mm.

quiz.q: A tool is consistent but always reads 2 mm too high. It is…
quiz.explain: Consistent but offset from the truth.

quiz.q: What is an interference fit?
options: A part pressed into a slightly smaller hole
quiz.explain: The shaft is slightly larger than the hole.

quiz.q: One inch equals exactly…

lessons.title: When things fail
lessons.summary: Fatigue, corrosion, creep and famous lessons.

cards.title: Overload
cards.text: The simplest failure: the load exceeds what the part can carry. Safety factors, good load estimates and checking for misuse prevent most of these.

cards.title: Fatigue

steps: Tiny crack at a stress point

cards.text: Repeated loading, even well below the breaking strength, can grow tiny cracks until a part snaps. Fatigue causes most mechanical failures in machines, aircraft and bridges.

cards.title: Beach marks
cards.text: Fatigue fractures often show curved "beach marks" on the broken surface, recording how the crack advanced, and a rougher final zone where it finally snapped.

cards.title: Corrosion
cards.text: Corrosion eats away metal, reducing its section and creating stress concentrations. Salt, water and dissimilar metals in contact speed it up.

cards.title: Creep
cards.text: Under constant load at high temperature, metals slowly stretch over time. Turbine blades and boiler tubes are designed for creep; even lead pipes and plastic shelves creep at room temperature.

cards.title: The Comet airliner
cards.text: The de Havilland Comet, the first jet airliner, suffered fatal crashes in 1954 caused by metal fatigue starting at the corners of square openings in its pressurised cabin. Rounded windows became standard.

cards.title: The 2001 Entre-os-Rios bridge collapse
cards.text: In March 2001, a pier of the Hintze Ribeiro bridge over the Douro collapsed, killing 59 people. Years of riverbed erosion, aggravated by sand extraction, had undermined its foundation. Portugal tightened bridge inspections afterwards.

cards.title: Human and organisational factors

items: Design checks by a second engineer

cards.text: Many failures come from design errors, poor maintenance, skipped inspections or ignored warnings, not just materials. Good engineering includes checking and learning from near-misses.

cards.title: Redundancy
cards.text: Critical systems have backups so one failure doesn't cause disaster: multiple cables on a bridge, two engines on airliners, extra bolts in a joint.

cards.title: Root cause analysis
cards.text: After a failure, engineers ask "why?" repeatedly to reach the underlying cause, not just the broken part. Fixing only the symptom lets it happen again.

quiz.q: What causes most mechanical failures in machines and aircraft?
Why did the Comet airliner crashes lead to rounded windows?
options: Square corners concentrated stress and started fatigue cracks

quiz.q: What is creep?
options: Slow permanent stretching under constant load, especially when hot

lessons.title: The engineering design process
lessons.summary: From problem to working product.

cards.title: Start with the problem

items: Who will use and maintain it?

cards.text: Good design starts by defining the problem and the requirements clearly: what must it do, under what conditions, at what cost, by when? A great solution to the wrong problem is worthless.

cards.title: The design cycle
cards.text: Design is iterative: define, generate ideas, choose, build a prototype, test, learn, improve. Several loops are normal.

cards.title: Requirements: must vs nice
cards.text: Separate must-haves from nice-to-haves. A clear list helps choose between options and stops scope creep.

cards.title: Concept selection
cards.text: Engineers compare options with a decision matrix: score each concept against weighted criteria like cost, weight, reliability and ease of manufacture.

cards.title: Prototyping

viz.unit: relative cost to fix a problem (illustrative)

cards.text: Build quick, cheap prototypes to learn early: cardboard, 3D prints, breadboards. Failing early costs little; failing after production costs a lot.

cards.title: Testing
cards.text: Tests check the design meets its requirements, including extremes: heat, cold, vibration, water, misuse. Many products are tested to failure to learn their real limits.

cards.title: Trade-offs
cards.text: Every design balances competing goals: lighter often means more expensive; stronger often means heavier; cheaper may mean shorter life. The engineer's job is the best balance for the purpose.

cards.title: Standards and codes
cards.text: Standards (EN, ISO, IEC) capture decades of lessons. Following them makes products safer, compatible and legally sellable, like CE marking in Europe.

cards.title: Documentation
cards.text: Drawings, calculations, test reports and decisions must be recorded so others can build, check, maintain and improve the design later.

cards.title: Systems thinking
cards.text: A product is a system of parts that interact. Changing one part, such as a bigger motor, can affect power supply, heat, weight and cost elsewhere. Systems engineering keeps the whole in view.

quiz.q: When is fixing a design problem cheapest?
quiz.explain: Costs multiply at each later stage.

quiz.q: What is a decision matrix used for?
options: Comparing design concepts against weighted criteria

quiz.q: What does CE marking indicate?
options: Conformity with EU safety and other requirements
